chapter_summary:
Once you have a fully constructed skeleton with properly oriented joints, the next critical step is **skinning**. Skinning is the process of attaching your 3D character's mesh (the geometry) to its underlying skeletal rig. Without skinning, the skeleton would move independently, and the mesh would remain static. The goal of skinning is to make the mesh deform realistically as the joints move, mimicking the way muscles and skin stretch and compress over bones. In Maya, the most common and versatile method for character skinning is **smooth binding**.

To perform a smooth bind, you first select the skeleton's root joint (or all relevant joints) and then, while holding Shift, select the geometry you wish to bind. Then, navigate to **Rigging > Skin > Bind Skin** (open the options box). Inside the options, you'll find several important settings. "Bind To" should usually be set to "Selected Joints" or "Joint Hierarchy." "Bind Method" is often "Closest Distance" or "Geodesic Voxel," with Geodesic Voxel often providing better initial results for complex meshes. "Max Influences" is a crucial setting; it determines how many joints can influence a single vertex. A value of 3 or 4 is common for characters, meaning each vertex will be influenced by a maximum of 3 or 4 nearby joints. Too many influences can make painting weights difficult and increase calculation time, while too few can lead to rigid, unnatural deformations. "Dropoff Rate" controls how quickly a joint's influence diminishes with distance. After configuring these settings, click "Bind Skin."

Upon binding, Maya automatically assigns **skin weights** to each vertex on your mesh. A skin weight is a numerical value (from 0 to 1) that determines how much a particular joint influences a specific vertex. A weight of 1 means the joint has full influence over that vertex, while a weight of 0 means no influence. The sum of all weights for a single vertex must always equal 1. Maya's automatic weighting is a good starting point, but it rarely produces perfect deformations, especially in areas like shoulders, elbows, knees, and hips. This is where the **Paint Skin Weights Tool** becomes indispensable.

You can access the Paint Skin Weights Tool by selecting your skinned mesh and going to **Rigging > Skin > Paint Skin Weights Tool** (or by right-clicking the mesh and choosing "Paint > Skin Weights"). This tool allows you to visually paint weight values directly onto your mesh. In the tool settings, you'll see a list of all influencing joints. By selecting a joint, you can then paint its influence onto the mesh using various brush modes (e.g., "Add," "Replace," "Smooth"). "Replace" mode is used to set a specific weight value, "Add" mode increases the weight, and "Smooth" mode averages the weights of surrounding vertices, which is excellent for blending deformations and removing sharp creases. It's often helpful to turn on "Color Ramp" in the tool settings, which visually represents weights with a gradient (e.g., blue for 0 influence, red for 1 influence).

Common mistakes during skinning often involve **collapsing geometry** (vertices pulling into the wrong place) or **unwanted bulges/pinching** in areas of high deformation. These usually indicate incorrect weight distribution. For example, if a shoulder joint is influencing vertices far down the arm, rotating the shoulder will cause the arm to collapse. To fix this, you would select the shoulder joint in the Paint Skin Weights Tool and paint *down* its influence (e.g., using "Replace" mode with a value of 0, or "Smooth") on the unwanted vertices, then paint *up* the influence of the correct joint (e.g., the upper arm joint) on those same vertices. Always work symmetrically if your character is symmetrical by enabling "Mirror Skin Weights" (Rigging > Skin > Mirror Skin Weights) or using symmetry options within the painting tool. Before binding, ensure your mesh has clean topology, frozen transformations (Modify > Freeze Transformations), and deleted history (Edit > Delete All By Type > History). These steps prevent many common skinning headaches and ensure a stable bind.

screens.title: Skinning: Bind Geometry to Joints
screens.subtitle: Attach your character mesh to a skeleton so motion produces realistic deformation.

narration.text: In this lesson we'll learn what skinning does, why it is essential for believable character motion, and which Maya tools professionals use to get it right. Skinning connects geometry to a rig so the mesh follows joint movement; without it a skeleton moves while the mesh remains static. Smooth bind is Maya's common method for organic characters because it lets multiple joints influence each vertex, producing blended, muscle-like deformation. You will see how bind options like Bind Method, Max Influences, and Dropoff Rate shape initial weights, and why automatic weights are a starting point rather than the final pass. We will also explore the Paint Skin Weights Tool, where you paint joint influence, use Replace/Add/Smooth modes, and turn on a color ramp to visualize weights. Finally, I'll walk you through a hands-on cylinder arm binding and show how to correct collapsing geometry and unwanted bulges by adjusting weights and mirroring. By the end you will understand the full bind workflow and know which tool to reach for when a knee or shoulder deforms poorly. Keep an eye out for symmetry and clean topology — they save a lot of rework.

screens.title: What is Skinning?
screens.subtitle: Definition, goals, and the role skinning plays in animation

narration.text: Skinning is the process of attaching a mesh to an underlying skeleton so the geometry deforms as joints move. The goal is realistic deformation: when a joint rotates, nearby vertices should follow in proportions that mimic skin and muscle rather than snapping rigidly to a single bone. In Maya this is done by assigning skin weights — numerical values between zero and one — to each vertex for the influencing joints, with the weights across a vertex adding to one. A practical example is a character elbow: multiple joints around the shoulder, upper arm and forearm typically contribute to the bend. Without blended weights the elbow would collapse or create sharp creases. A common misconception is to expect automatic binding to be final. In practice automatic weights give you a starting distribution, but you must inspect and refine especially around joints that bend a lot. Why this matters: animation depends on reliable deformation; sloppy skinning forces animators to compensate and wastes time. When you think skinning, think attach, weight, test, and refine. Ask yourself after a bind: does rotation produce smooth, predictable motion or does the mesh pinch or pull? That check directs your next painting pass.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Skinning assigns vertex weights so a mesh moves with a rig and deforms organically during animation.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is Skinning?
Skinning
Attach mesh to a skeleton and assign weights so deformation looks organic during joint motion.
Key properties:
  • Weights per vertex are in the range 0 to 1 and sum to 1.
  • Multiple joints can influence a vertex for blended deformation.
  • Automatic bind gives a starting state that usually needs refinement.
Key Takeaway

Skinning is the bridge between a rig and believable mesh motion: it must be tested and refined, not assumed correct.

Visual explanation
Vertex weight example
// conceptual per-vertex weights Vertex A: shoulder 0.6, upperArm 0.4, others 0.0 Vertex B: upperArm 0.2, elbow 0.8 Sum per vertex = 1.0
These numbers determine how much each joint moves the vertex when animated.
Concrete example
For an elbow bend, blend influence between the upper arm and forearm joints. If one joint has full influence the mesh will collapse or crease sharply; blended weights create a smooth arc.

screens.title: Performing a Smooth Bind in Maya
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step bind workflow and critical options to set

narration.text: Executing a smooth bind in Maya is a predictable sequence: prepare geometry, select joints, set bind options, and run the bind. First, prepare the mesh by ensuring clean topology, freezing transformations, and deleting history. These prevent unexpected offsets or misapplied weights. Next, select the root joint or the joints you want to bind, then Shift-select the mesh. Open Rigging > Skin > Bind Skin options. Key options to set: Bind To should use Selected Joints or Joint Hierarchy depending on whether you chose a set or entire chain. Bind Method choices include Closest Distance and Geodesic Voxel; Geodesic Voxel often gives better initial results for complex meshes because it evaluates voxelized volume distance rather than surface distance. Set Max Influences to a manageable number like three or four to limit how many joints affect any vertex. Dropoff Rate controls how influence decays with distance and is useful for tuning initial falloff. After applying Bind Skin, immediately rotate several joints to test the deformation. If there are glaring problems, use the Paint Skin Weights Tool to fix them. A common misconception is to think Bind Method doesn't matter — in reality it often determines whether an initial pass needs minimal tweaking or extensive painting. Your test rotations tell you how much painting is required.

keyIdea.title: Bind workflow
keyIdea.text: Prepare, choose proper Bind Method, set Max Influences, apply bind, then test and refine with weight painting.

content.html:
Process › Performing a Smooth Bind
Step-by-step bind
Follow these checked steps to produce a clean initial bind.
1. Prepare geometry
Freeze transforms, delete history, and ensure even topology so weights interpolate predictably.
2. Select joints and mesh
Select root joint or joint set, then Shift-select the mesh to bind to those joints.
3. Set Bind Options
Choose Bind To, Bind Method (Geodesic Voxel recommended for complex meshes), Max Influences (3–4), and Dropoff Rate.
4. Bind and test
Click Bind Skin and immediately rotate joints to surface-test deformations and locate problem areas.
Key Takeaway

A careful bind with the right options reduces weight painting time and yields more natural deformations.

Options explained
Bind To: Selected Joints or Joint Hierarchy — choose based on selection scope.
Bind Method: Closest Distance vs Geodesic Voxel — Geodesic Voxel often improves initial weights on complex volumes.
Max Influences: Limit joint count per vertex to balance deformation quality and painting complexity.
Quick test
Rotate shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints after binding. Note pinching or collapsing and target those areas in the Paint Skin Weights Tool.

screens.title: Bind Method: Closest Distance vs Geodesic Voxel
screens.subtitle: How the method affects initial weight distribution

narration.text: Bind Method controls how Maya computes initial distances between vertices and joints during a smooth bind. The commonly used options are Closest Distance and Geodesic Voxel. Closest Distance assesses surface distance from vertex to joint and can be fast for simple, fairly flat meshes. Geodesic Voxel computes a volumetric approximation that better respects mesh volume, often producing cleaner initial assignments for limbs, torsos, and meshes with thickness. A concrete example: a character arm with a hollow sleeve may get mismatched weights with Closest Distance because surface projections cross the sleeve; Geodesic Voxel understands the volume better and typically avoids transferring influence across thin surfaces. A misconception is assuming one method is always superior; instead choose based on the mesh complexity. After binding with either method you must test joint rotations and examine problematic areas such as shoulders and hips. If you still see incorrect influence, the Paint Skin Weights Tool is the corrective step. In short, Bind Method sets the starting point and can reduce painting time when chosen appropriately. Bind Method: Closest Distance vs Geodesic Voxel means bind method sets initial weight calculation; geodesic voxel generally gives better results for thick, complex meshes.. In practical terms, how the method affects initial weight distribution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bind Method impact
keyIdea.text: Bind Method sets initial weight calculation; Geodesic Voxel generally gives better results for thick, complex meshes.

content.html:
Comparison › Bind Method
Closest Distance
Surface-based distance; fast and effective on simple surfaces but can misassign across thin geometry.
  • Fast calculation.
  • May transfer influence across thin gaps.
  • Good for simple meshes and when performance matters.
Geodesic Voxel
Voxel-based volume approach; better for complex or thick meshes and often reduces manual fixes.
  • Respects mesh volume for more accurate initial weights.
  • Slightly slower but often saves time in painting.
  • Recommended for limbs, torsos, and characters with thickness.
Example
An arm inside a sleeve: Closest Distance may let shoulder influence show inside the sleeve; Geodesic Voxel typically respects the sleeve's volume and assigns cleaner weights.
Takeaway
Choose the method based on mesh complexity; test and then paint to refine.

screens.title: Skin Weights: Numbers that drive deformation
screens.subtitle: What weights represent and the invariant that guides painting

narration.text: Skin weights are scalar values assigned per vertex that describe how much each joint influences that vertex during deformation. Each weight lies between zero and one, and the weights for all influencing joints at a single vertex always sum to one. This invariant is fundamental because it guarantees predictable interpolation: when a joint rotates, the vertex's new position is a weighted blend of joint transforms. A concrete example: if a vertex has 0.7 weight from the upper arm joint and 0.3 from the shoulder joint, most motion follows the upper arm but a bit comes from the shoulder, creating a smooth transition. A misconception to avoid is thinking a weight of zero means the vertex is unconstrained; it simply means that particular joint does not contribute. When you paint, remember to preserve the sum-to-one behavior by reducing one influence before increasing another or use the painting modes that enforce normalization. Practically, keeping Max Influences modest simplifies the system — fewer numbers to manage per vertex — while still allowing smooth blending where it matters. Skin Weights: Numbers that drive deformation means weights are normalized per-vertex values; their sum equals one and they determine the blend of joint transforms.. In practical terms, what weights represent and the invariant that guides painting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Weights math
keyIdea.text: Weights are normalized per-vertex values; their sum equals one and they determine the blend of joint transforms.

content.html:
Definition › Skin Weights
Skin Weights explained
Weights determine how vertex positions are computed as a blend of joint transforms.
Invariant: weights for a vertex sum to 1.0, ensuring consistent blending.
Example: Vertex V = 0.7*UpperArm + 0.3*Shoulder produces a softer elbow curve than a single-joint influence.
Practice: Limit Max Influences to simplify painting; use Smooth brush to average neighbors for stable blends.
Common misconception
Automatic weights equal final weights. They are a starting point; high-deformation areas require careful painting.
Concrete number example
Vertex: shoulder 0.2 | upperArm 0.8 | sum = 1.0
Key Takeaway

Treat weights as normalized blending factors; paint to redistribute influence and keep the sum consistent.

screens.title: Using the Paint Skin Weights Tool
screens.subtitle: How to visually paint and refine joint influence

narration.text: The Paint Skin Weights Tool lets you interactively adjust how joints influence vertices by painting values directly on the mesh. Open it after selecting a skinned mesh via Rigging > Skin > Paint Skin Weights Tool. In the tool's list you'll see all influencing joints; select one and paint its influence using three common brush modes. Replace mode sets a precise weight value to painted vertices and is useful for removing unwanted influence. Add mode increases the selected joint's weight, helpful when a joint needs a stronger presence. Smooth mode averages weights across neighboring vertices to create soft transitions and remove creases. Turn on the Color Ramp visualization to see weights as a gradient—often blue for zero influence and red for full influence—so you can spot problem areas. A concrete workflow: select the problem joint, use Replace with value zero on vertices that should not be influenced, then paint Add or Smooth for the correct joint nearby until the bend looks natural. Always test the joint rotation after painting. A common mistake is painting without checking normalization; rely on Maya's normalization but watch for artifacts where many influences overlap.

keyIdea.title: Paint workflow
keyIdea.text: Use Replace, Add, and Smooth modes and a color ramp to correct influence visually and test by rotating joints.

content.html:
Process › Paint Skin Weights Tool
Interactive painting
Select a joint then paint its influence using modes designed for precise control.
Brush modes
  • Replace: set a specific weight value; useful for removing unwanted influence.
  • Add: increase the selected joint's weight where more influence is needed.
  • Smooth: average neighbor weights to remove sharp transitions and creases.
Visualization
Enable Color Ramp to see a gradient representing 0 to 1 influence and quickly find problem vertices.
Pro tip

Work on one joint at a time: reduce wrong influence first, then build correct influence for the desired joint.

Example workflow
If the shoulder pulls the forearm, select the shoulder joint, paint Replace with zero on the forearm vertices, then select the forearm joint and Add influence where appropriate.
Color Ramp
Blue = 0 influence, red = 1 influence. Use this to guide where to paint or smooth.

screens.title: Brush Modes: Replace, Add, Smooth
screens.subtitle: When and why to use each brush mode

narration.text: Each brush mode in the Paint Skin Weights Tool serves a different corrective role. Replace is deterministic: it writes a precise weight value to vertices regardless of existing values. Use Replace when you must eliminate an unwanted joint influence completely or set a region to an exact value. Add increments the selected joint's weight and is helpful when you want to strengthen influence without overwriting neighboring data; its incremental nature can be safer for subtle corrections. Smooth averages weight values across neighboring vertices. Smooth is your go-to for blending transitions and removing sharp creases that appear after heavy Replace or Add passes. A common workflow is to use Replace to remove erroneous influence, Add to rebuild correct influence, and Smooth as a finishing pass to blend transitions. A misconception is relying on only Add or only Smooth; effective correction often uses the three modes in sequence and tests with joint rotation between passes. Always observe the summed influences and test the actual joint motion to confirm the change produced the intended deformation. Brush Modes: Replace, Add, Smooth means use replace to set values, add to build influence, and smooth to blend — combine them in sequence for reliable fixes.. In practical terms, when and why to use each brush mode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Brush strategy
keyIdea.text: Use Replace to set values, Add to build influence, and Smooth to blend — combine them in sequence for reliable fixes.

content.html:
Comparison › Brush Modes
Brush modes in practice
Match brush choice to the correction you need and test often.
Replace
Set an exact weight value to remove wrong influence quickly.
Add
Incrementally increase the selected joint's influence in small amounts.
Smooth
Average neighbors to remove creases and produce gradual transitions.
Sequence example
Replace (clear wrong influence) → Add (build correct influence) → Smooth (blend transitions). Test rotation between each step.
Common mistake

Relying only on Smooth will rarely fix a wrong influence assignment; it blends existing values rather than removing them.

screens.title: Max Influences & Dropoff Rate
screens.subtitle: Balancing influence count and falloff for manageable painting

narration.text: Max Influences and Dropoff Rate are crucial bind settings that affect both deformation quality and your workload when painting weights. Max Influences limits how many joints can affect each vertex. A typical value is three or four; fewer influences simplify painting because there are fewer numbers to balance per vertex, but too few can produce rigid, less natural results. Dropoff Rate determines how quickly a joint's influence decays with distance and affects the spread of a joint's weight across nearby vertices. A steep dropoff confines influence tightly around a joint, useful for mechanical or localized motion, while a shallow dropoff spreads influence farther, which can be good for soft transitions but may require additional cleanup to avoid unintended motion. A practical example: for a humanoid arm, Max Influences of 3 with a moderate dropoff often yields a good balance: the shoulder, upper arm, and elbow can contribute without overwhelming the vertex with distant joints. Misunderstanding these settings can lead to either excessive painting or insufficient blending; adjust them to match the model and then refine with painting. Max Influences & Dropoff Rate means max influences limits complexity; dropoff rate tunes how far a joint's influence extends. balance them for quality and manageability.. In practical terms, balancing influence count and falloff for manageable painting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Influence balance
keyIdea.text: Max Influences limits complexity; Dropoff Rate tunes how far a joint's influence extends. Balance them for quality and manageability.

content.html:
Core Setting › Max Influences & Dropoff
Max Influences
Restrict how many joints can influence any single vertex to keep painting manageable.
  • 3–4 is a common starting range for characters.
  • Lower values reduce complexity but may need extra painting in transitions.
  • Higher values increase smoothness potential but complicate painting and calculation time.
Dropoff Rate
Controls how rapidly influence decays with distance from a joint.
  • Steep dropoff confines influence to nearby vertices.
  • Shallow dropoff spreads influence and can smooth large deformations.
  • Adjust to mesh scale and test rotations to find the right feel.
Quick guideline

Start with Max Influences = 3 and a moderate Dropoff Rate. Increase or decrease based on test rotations and painting effort.

Example
An arm with Max Influences = 3 typically has shoulder, upper arm, and elbow influence at many vertices, giving a controllable and natural bend without distant joints interfering.

screens.title: Common Skinning Artifacts and Fixes
screens.subtitle: Collapsing geometry, bulges, and targeted painting strategies

narration.text: Common artifacts in skinning include collapsing geometry — where vertices pull inward toward the wrong joint — and bulges or pinching around high-deformation areas. Collapsing often results from a joint influencing vertices that should belong to a different joint. For example, if the shoulder joint influences vertices far down the arm, rotating the shoulder will pull the forearm inward. The direct fix is to use the Paint Skin Weights Tool: select the shoulder joint and remove its influence on the offending vertices using Replace mode with a value of zero or Smooth to reduce its reach. Then select the correct joint, like the upper arm, and paint up its influence where needed. Bulges and pinching typically indicate abrupt weight transitions; apply Smooth to average neighbors and produce gradual blends. Another useful tool is Mirror Skin Weights when working on symmetric models because it lets you correct one side and copy weights across. A misconception is to assume mesh topology alone causes all artifacts; while topology matters, many visible issues are simply misassigned weights that painting can correct quickly if you target the right joints.

keyIdea.title: Artifact fixes
keyIdea.text: Collapsing geometry is typically a weight assignment issue—reduce wrong influence and reassign to the correct joint, then smooth.

content.html:
Definition › Artifacts & Fixes
Identify & correct
Use testing and painting to solve common artifacts rather than immediately remeshing.
Collapsing geometry
Cause: wrong joint influence reaching into adjacent regions. Fix: select the incorrect joint, Replace with 0 on affected vertices, then add influence to the correct joint and smooth.
Bulges & pinching
Cause: abrupt weight transitions. Fix: apply Smooth brush and refine local weights, check topology if smoothing doesn't help.
Quick diagnostic
Rotate the offending joint slowly. If far geometry moves, that joint's influence extends too far and must be reduced with painting.
Mirror weights
For symmetrical characters, use Mirror Skin Weights to copy corrections across axes and maintain parity between sides.

screens.title: Prepare Geometry and Skeleton Before Binding
screens.subtitle: Practical pre-bind checklist to avoid common failures

narration.text: Preparation prevents many skinning problems. Before binding, ensure your mesh has clean topology with consistent edge loops around deformation areas; this helps weights interpolate predictably when the mesh bends. Freeze transformations to reset translation, rotation and scale so the bind matrices are calculated from neutral transforms. Delete history to remove construction nodes that can interfere with a stable bind. Confirm joints are oriented correctly — for limbs it's common to orient the joint X-axis down the bone — because joint orientation affects rotation behavior and therefore how weights behave during animation. Check that the skeleton hierarchy is complete and that the root joint is selected if you plan to bind the whole chain. For a symmetrical model, verify naming conventions and symmetry across the axis so mirroring weights later is straightforward. A common misconception is that topology can be fixed after painting; while small fixes are possible, major topology changes usually require redoing the bind. Investing time in preparation saves far more time in weight painting and debugging later. Prepare Geometry and Skeleton Before Binding means freeze transforms, delete history, confirm joint orientation, and ensure clean topology to reduce bind-time problems.. In practical terms, practical pre-bind checklist to avoid common failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pre-bind checklist
keyIdea.text: Freeze transforms, delete history, confirm joint orientation, and ensure clean topology to reduce bind-time problems.

content.html:
Process › Preparation Checklist
Pre-bind Checklist
Complete these steps before binding to avoid costly rework.
Freeze Transformations
Reset translate/rotate/scale so the bind uses neutral transforms.
Delete History
Remove construction history that can alter deformation behavior unexpectedly.
Confirm Joint Orientation
Correct orientation keeps rotations predictable and reduces odd deformations at bends.
Topology checks
Ensure even edge loops around joints and adequate subdivisions where deformation must be smooth.
Why it matters

Proper preparation reduces time spent re-binding and painting, and produces more predictable animation-ready rigs.

screens.title: Lab: Skinning a Simple Cylinder Arm
screens.subtitle: Step-through the cylinder arm activity and refine the elbow bend

narration.text: This hands-on walkthrough ties together preparation, binding, and weight painting using a simple cylinder arm. Start by creating a cylinder and increasing Subdivisions Height to 10–15 so the bend looks smooth. Freeze Transformations and delete history on the cylinder. Create a three-joint chain: shoulder_JNT, elbow_JNT, wrist_JNT, positioned inside the cylinder and oriented X down the bone. Select shoulder_JNT then Shift-select the cylinder and open Rigging > Skin > Bind Skin. Set Bind Method to Geodesic Voxel and Max Influences to 3, then click Bind Skin. Rotate shoulder_JNT and elbow_JNT to observe deformation. If the top of the cylinder collapses or the elbow pinches, open the Paint Skin Weights Tool. Select shoulder_JNT and use Replace mode with value 0 on vertices that should not follow the shoulder. Select elbow_JNT and use Add plus Smooth to build a gradual zone of influence in the middle rows. Test rotation after small adjustments to see the effect immediately. Work symmetrically if the model has a mirrored side, and remember to save incremental versions. Hands-on Lab › Cylinder Arm Walkthrough
Steps to complete
Follow these steps in Maya and test rotation after each change.
  1. Create cylinder and set Subdivisions Height to 10–15. Freeze transforms and delete history.
  2. Create shoulder_JNT, elbow_JNT, wrist_JNT and orient joints with X along the bone.
  3. Select shoulder_JNT, Shift-select cylinder. Open Bind Skin options, use Geodesic Voxel, Max Influences = 3, then Bind Skin.
  4. Rotate joints to test. Open Paint Skin Weights Tool to correct any collapsing or pinching.
  5. Use Replace to remove wrong influence, Add to rebuild, and Smooth to blend. Re-test rotations after each pass.
Key Takeaway

Small, iterative painting steps with frequent testing produce reliable deformation faster than large, sweeping edits.

Scenario

Save strategy
Save incremental versions: prepare-bind, paint-pass-1, paint-pass-2. This makes it easy to revert if a painting change makes other areas worse.

screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from this chapter

narration.text: Let's consolidate three core ideas you should carry forward. First, skinning is the process that binds geometry to a rig through skin weights; treat automatic weights as a starting point and always test joint motion. Second, bind settings such as Bind Method, Max Influences and Dropoff Rate shape how much painting you will need; choose Geodesic Voxel for complex meshes and limit Max Influences to keep painting manageable. Third, the Paint Skin Weights Tool is your principal corrective instrument — use Replace to remove wrong influence, Add to build influence, and Smooth to blend. Practicing a prepare-bind-paint-test loop and using symmetry where possible will save you time and produce predictable deformations. These three concepts form a compact workflow you can apply to any character rig. narration.text: Finish with a short checklist you can apply to any skinning task. First, prepare your mesh: freeze transforms, delete history, and check joint orientation. These basic steps prevent many binding mistakes and make weights behave consistently. Second, choose bind options suited to your mesh: use Geodesic Voxel for volumetric accuracy on complex models and keep Max Influences low enough to make painting practical. Third, paint intentionally: remove incorrect influence first, then rebuild correct influence and finally smooth transitions. Use color ramp and symmetry to speed the process. These three reminders—prepare, choose, paint—form a compact routine that reduces iterations and gives you reliable deformation results. What to Remember › Practice Checklist
Prepare
Freeze transforms, delete history, and confirm joint orientation before binding.
Choose
Pick Bind Method and Max Influences appropriate to mesh complexity to reduce painting effort.
Paint
Remove wrong influence, add correct influence, smooth blends, test by rotating joints, and mirror when possible.

A small, repeatable practice routine will make your binds faster and more reliable than chasing perfect automatic weights.
